opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think my view has shifted quite a bit. Early on, I was drawn to iterative refinement almost as an intuition borrowed from how people learn: you try something, you see where it falls short, and you go back and fix it. That framing showed up a lot in my thinking about things like iterated learning and forgetting-and-relearning, where repeatedly resetting and retraining parts of a network seemed to push it toward simpler, more generalizable solutions. There was something appealing about the idea that the process of revisiting, rather than just the final objective, shapes what a model ends up representing.

What's changed is that I've become more careful about what "refinement" actually buys you. With large language models, it's tempting to assume that if you let a model critique and revise its own output, it'll steadily get better. Sometimes it does, but often the gains come from the model having access to some new signal, like an external check, a tool, a verifier, or just more structured decomposition of the problem, rather than from refinement in and of itself. Without that grounding, a model can just as easily talk itself into a confident wrong answer, or drift away from something that was correct to begin with.

So I now think of iterative refinement less as a general-purpose improvement loop and more as a way of creating opportunities for the right information to enter the process. The interesting questions become: what does each iteration expose the model to that it didn't have before, and what inductive bias does repeating the process introduce? When you design it with that in mind, refinement can be really powerful. When you treat it as magic, you mostly just spend more compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's shifted quite a bit. When I started thinking about this, I was pretty excited about the idea that you could just have a model look at its own output, critique it, and then produce a better version. It felt almost like a free lunch. You take the same model, you spend more compute at inference time, and you get a better answer. And there were enough early demos where that worked that it was easy to believe it generalized.

What changed my mind was actually trying to pin down when it works and when it doesn't. The thing I kept running into is that refinement only helps if the model can recognize a mistake it couldn't avoid making in the first place. That's a pretty specific condition. For some tasks it's true. Checking an arithmetic step is easier than generating the whole derivation, so a model can catch its own slip. But for a lot of things, generation and verification are basically the same skill. If the model wrote a wrong answer because it genuinely believes it, asking it to reflect just produces a confident justification of the same wrong answer. You get this convergence toward whatever the model already thought, dressed up as having been checked.

So I've moved from thinking of iterative refinement as a general-purpose capability amplifier to thinking of it as something that's really about the structure of the problem. The useful question isn't "can the model refine?" It's "is there an asymmetry here between how hard it is to produce a good answer and how hard it is to tell a good answer from a bad one?" When that gap exists, refinement is great, and you can even get better returns by giving the model an external signal, like running the code or checking against a tool, rather than relying on pure self-reflection. When the gap doesn't exist, you're mostly burning tokens.

The other thing I've come to appreciate is that a lot of what looked like refinement gains early on was really just sampling. If you generate a few candidates and pick one, you'll often do better, and it's easy to attribute that to the "reflection" step when it's really the variance doing the work. Once you control for that carefully, the pure self-correction effect is often smaller than people hoped.

So I'd say I'm less of a believer in the romantic version, where the model sits there thinking harder and gets wiser, and more interested in the engineering version. Where can we find or construct a verifier that's genuinely more reliable than the generator? That's where the real leverage is, and it's a more honest framing of what's actually going on.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more careful about separating iteration from improvement. It’s tempting to think that if you let a model revisit an answer, critique it, and try again, the answer will keep getting better. But that depends on whether it can actually recognize what went wrong. Otherwise, you can end up with something that sounds more convincing without being more correct.

So the question for me has shifted from “How many rounds of refinement should we do?” to “What useful feedback does each round provide?” If there’s a test you can run or some independent signal you can check, there’s a much clearer path to improvement. I’m still excited about iterative refinement, but I see the feedback mechanism as the central piece, rather than iteration itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more interested in what makes refinement actually work. It’s tempting to imagine that you can take an answer, ask the model to improve it, and keep getting something better. But another iteration doesn’t necessarily give you new information. Sometimes you just get a more polished version of the same mistake.

So the question for me is: where is the feedback coming from? If you can run a test, interact with an environment, or check the answer against some independent signal, then refinement has something concrete to work with. If the model is simply judging its own response, you have to ask whether it can recognize the error it couldn’t avoid in the first place.

I still think it’s a promising way to spend additional computation. But I’d put less emphasis on the number of iterations and more on the quality of the feedback and whether you can reliably select a better result.
